title: 5 Essential Strategies For The First Day Of School https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2016/07/30/5-essential-strategies-for-the-first-day-of-school/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin lays out five strategies for creating a first-day-of-school experience that gives a teacher leverage for the rest of the year. He recommends greeting every student individually at the door, sharing a personal or quirky story to build likability, teaching the first routine with unusually meticulous modeling since it sets the excellence bar for everything after, framing the classroom management plan as existing to protect students' right to learn, and teaching a genuinely challenging academic lesson on day one to signal that hard work and fun coexist. He argues these five moves together set students' expectations exactly where the teacher wants them, avoiding a year spent begging, bribing, and prodding students to reach that standard later. The piece closes by tying the strategies back to SCM's broader philosophy that student enjoyment of the classroom is what gives a management plan real meaning.
points: Greet every student individually at the door on day one to put them at ease and start building rapport immediately.
Share a personal or quirky story early to boost likability, which Linsin calls crucial leverage for classroom management.
Teach the very first routine with exceptional, detailed modeling, since it sets the excellence bar for everything after.
Frame the classroom management plan explicitly as existing to protect students, not to control them.
Teach a genuinely challenging academic lesson on the first day to show that fun and hard work coexist in your room.
quotes: As your students enter your classroom for the first time, stop each one at the door and say hello.

Your likability is crucial to effective classroom management, and nothing breaks down walls, creates ready-made leverage, and draws students into your circle of influence faster or more powerfully than telling a story.
Your first routine of the year is the most important routine of the year.
To that end, explain that the sole purpose of your rules and consequences is to protect their right to learn and enjoy school. The plan is meant for them , not you.
Let them experience legitimate success—perhaps on a scale they never have before—and a deeper appreciation for learning.
It’s to set your expectations precisely where you want them to be so you don’t have to struggle for the rest of the year trying to prod, beg, lecture, bribe, and implore your students to get there.
